headline: Inference is becoming *load-aware*: the stack now fits itself to the traffic.
subhead: Seven levers can move with the load, from which model answers to how deep each token goes. Coding agents are what make re-tuning them affordable.
intro: Serving a large language model means a chain of decisions: which model answers, which machine takes the request, how a cluster splits reading prompts from writing answers, how generation is sped up, how much computation each token gets, and how it runs on a particular chip. Each was set once, by hand. During 2026 they began to move with the load: with what is being asked, by whom, on what hardware. Coding agents made that affordable by taking over the tuning. This page maps the levers and how they connect, tracks who has each one working and what it has bought, and checks the claims against the evidence, including your own reading of it. An agent re-examines it every day.

picture.head: Seven levers can move with the load
picture.text: Which model answers, which machine takes it, how the cluster is split, how tokens are written, how the engine runs, what the model is, and how deep each token goes. Four run in production.

picture.head: Twenty-five teams described or updated a loop since mid-October
picture.text: Agents that profile an engine, rewrite part of it, measure, and keep what wins. Providers, open engines, chip vendors, academics and individuals. Thirty-five more described versions earlier.

picture.head: The prompt cache ties the levers together
picture.text: Nine-tenths of agent tokens are re-read context, cached per model and per machine. That is why routing is sticky and why the model is chosen once per session.

picture.head: Measuring is now harder than optimising
picture.text: Kernel speed-ups of several times shrink to almost nothing inside a full engine. Some agent runs game the benchmark. Patches arrive faster than people can review them.

picture.head: Not yet recursive, and the commons keeps up
picture.text: The loops are bounded hillclimbs with goals set by people; nothing compounds yet. Specialised wins reach vLLM and SGLang within weeks, and per-customer tuning has bought tens of percent.

claims.statement: Given a harness built by people, coding agents now find and land inference optimisations that survive end-to-end measurement in production engines.
claims.plain: This is not autocomplete for CUDA. Agents are finding bottlenecks a senior engineer would be pleased to find, and the patches are being merged.
claims.why: If true, the supply of performance engineering stops being limited by the few hundred people who can do it. If false, everything else here is marketing.

history.why: Founding estimate. Merged public pull requests in vLLM and SGLang carry it; independent benchmarks showing parity at best on isolated kernels, and search beating agents on configuration, hold it down.

claims.raise_if: An independent group reproduces a vendor's agent-found gain, or a benchmark with end-to-end scoring shows agents beating shipped kernels in LLM serving by a clear margin.
claims.lower_if: Merged agent-written optimisations get reverted for correctness, or matched-budget search keeps beating agents as budgets and models grow.

claims.short: What you have sets the optimum
claims.statement: The best serving configuration depends on what you are running: the traffic shape, the model and the chip. Kernels and settings tuned for one combination leave double-digit gains unclaimed on another, and all three keep changing.
claims.plain: There is no best way to serve a model, only a best way to serve this traffic, with this model, on this chip. Change any one and the old best stops being best.
claims.why: This is the centre of your framing: a stack that fits itself to what you have. If one good general recipe existed, there would be nothing for a loop to chase.

history.why: Founding estimate. Supported from many directions, including independent measurement. Held below 0.9 because nearly all of it comes from one workload class and one public trace set.
Scope widened the same day, after the reader said local means fitted to what you have. Per-device evidence that sat under the retired C8 now counts here. Confidence unchanged.

claims.raise_if: A second public workload that is not coding agents, or a second chip family, shows a different set of winning optimisations under like-for-like measurement.
claims.lower_if: Engines tuned on AgentX and NVIDIA hardware turn out near-optimal on other workloads and chips too, meaning one good general recipe exists after all.

claims.statement: Tuning the stack to one customer's own traffic is worth enough over a well-tuned class-level stack to justify doing it per customer, continuously.
claims.plain: Your workload gets its own engine build. This is the part of user-workload-aware that is still a bet.
claims.why: It decides whether the value sits with whoever holds each customer's traffic, or in shared engines that everyone gets for free.

history.why: Founding estimate. The like-for-like numbers that exist are 20 to 45%, recipes are reported to transfer between customers, and a general engine came within 6% of a bespoke one. The case for is that a bespoke engine now costs a couple of hundred GPU-hours.

Correction after reading Modal first-hand. Its 20% came from tuning a drafter to the coding-agent class, and its recipe carried over to other models, not customers. One founding reason against was a misreading. Per-customer drafter gains are 34 to 45% on different baselines; there is still no same-endpoint comparison.

claims.raise_if: A provider publishes same-endpoint numbers showing per-customer tuning beating its own class-level stack by more than about 1.5x, or the cost of a bespoke engine keeps falling.
claims.lower_if: More reports that recipes transfer between customers, or upstream engines closing announced private leads within a quarter.

claims.statement: Proposing optimisations has become cheap. Knowing whether one is real (on realistic inputs, end to end, with outputs intact) is the binding constraint, together with the human review that still gates what ships.
claims.plain: The agent is not the hard part. The rig that catches a fake speed-up is.
claims.why: Whoever owns the best evaluation rig, or the traffic to build one, owns the loop. It also tells you which published numbers to discount.

history.why: Founding estimate. The vendors building the loops and the independent benchmarks criticising them say the same thing, with numbers. The one complication is that a public benchmark let outsiders compete without private traffic.

claims.raise_if: More merged regressions traced to weak gates, or providers competing on evaluation infrastructure instead of on agents.
claims.lower_if: A cheap, general oracle appears (for example simulated traffic that predicts production), or isolated kernel results start transferring end to end.

claims.statement: The optimisation loop is becoming recursive: the models being served power the agents that optimise their serving, the agents improve their own process, and gains compound from one cycle to the next.
claims.plain: This is the RSI claim. Today the first part is true, the second is mostly aspiration, and the third has not been shown by anyone.
claims.why: Compounding is the difference between a useful tool and a runaway advantage for whoever starts first.

history.why: Founding estimate. Models do serve their own optimisers, and two groups recycle search traces into training. Against that: curated knowledge made one production system worse, more time did not help agents in a benchmark, and the label is being attached to systems with no self-improvement in them.

claims.raise_if: A published curve where gain per cycle rises, or a model trained on optimisation traces that out-optimises its teacher on a production task.
claims.lower_if: Loops plateau after the first few rounds on each new model, or inherited agent memory keeps hurting in ablations.

claims.statement: New model architectures and new chips now arrive faster than people can hand-tune for them. That, more than agent capability, is what makes an automated loop necessary.
claims.plain: By the time a person has tuned the kernels, traffic has moved to the next model. Something has to do day-zero support, and it will not be a person.
claims.why: It explains the timing, and for a provider serving many models it is the daily problem: every new model needs a drafter, a tuned engine and a correctness check before the traffic arrives.

history.why: Founding estimate. Several independent accounts of the same pressure, including on chips with no kernel ecosystem. The main statistic behind it is one vendor's citation, and one new model reached near-parity by hand integration.

claims.raise_if: Time from a model's release to a tuned public result keeps shrinking and is credited to agents, or more non-NVIDIA chips reach parity through agent-written kernels.
claims.lower_if: Architectures converge again, or one vendor library covers new models well enough at release.

claims.statement: Open engines absorb specialised wins within weeks, so a private performance lead over upstream vLLM or SGLang is short-lived.
claims.plain: If you can wait a month, you get most of it for free.
claims.why: This is the question of who keeps the gains: providers as margin, or everyone as cheaper tokens.

history.why: Founding estimate. Both open engines run agent loops themselves and take fixes upstream fast. Two providers claim private leads of roughly 2x that nobody outside has checked.

claims.raise_if: Announced private leads are matched by public runs within a quarter.
claims.lower_if: Those leads persist or widen, or key optimisations stop going upstream.

claims.short: The loop reaches hardware you own
claims.statement: The same self-tuning loop will run on stacks the user owns (a workstation, an on-prem box, a laptop), tuned to that user's own usage, not only in provider clusters.
claims.plain: This is the local in your framing. Today local stacks tune themselves to the device, once, by trying existing settings. Nothing tunes itself to you.
claims.why: It is the part of the reader's framing with the least support, so it is either the open ground or the mistake.

history.why: Founding estimate. One paper shows agent-written kernels on edge chips; everything else local is one-off autotuning or hand work. Cost analyses run against it, and the loop's economics lean on batching that a single user lacks.

claims.raise_if: An agent-driven loop on owned hardware shows a like-for-like gain from the owner's own traffic, or private fleets that are not hyperscalers publish such results.
claims.lower_if: Local runtimes keep converging on vendor compilers and one-off autotuning, and cost analyses keep favouring shared capacity.
claims.retired_why: Retired the day it was opened. It tested whether the loop reaches on-device hardware, which is not what the reader meant by local. The part that matters, the stack fitting whatever chip it finds, now sits under C2.

claims.short: Open and frontier models share the work
claims.statement: Open-weight and frontier models coexist behind one harness. Routine sessions go to a cheaper open model and hard ones to a frontier model, and the prompt cache decides how often that choice can be made.
claims.plain: Nobody picks one model any more. Something picks per session, and it cannot change its mind mid-session without paying to re-read everything.
claims.why: For a provider this sets what you serve. Open models carry most of the tokens and about a quarter of the money, and the routing decision is a product you can own or lose to the harness.

history.why: Opened when the reader widened the frame. Coexistence is measured on two gateways and shipped by five products. Held down because an independent test found routers do not beat a fixed cheap model, and a static swap may capture most of the saving.

A router vendor's own public board shows single models from its pool beating its coding router on quality and cost on public coding tasks, a second result after AutoBench. The cache part holds: that router stayed on one model nine turns in ten.

claims.raise_if: An independent agentic benchmark, with caching priced in, shows a shipped router beating the best fixed model on cost at equal quality.
claims.lower_if: Open models stall or frontier prices fall so that one model is simply best, or more products drop automatic routing.

claims.short: The model itself becomes a setting
claims.statement: Tuning an open model to one domain or harness (post-training, reinforcement learning, distillation) works as an inference optimisation: a smaller tuned model does a narrow job at lower cost and latency than a general one.
claims.plain: Instead of making a big model run faster, you make a small one good enough at your one job.
claims.why: For a provider this is the lever with the most lock-in and the shortest shelf life. A tuned model needs its own drafter and its own compiled engine, and it is tied to a base model that may be withdrawn within months.

history.why: Opened when the reader widened the frame. Named customers report real gains on narrow tasks, one measured by a third party. Against that: a tuner's own table shows a newer general model beating its tuned one, a frontier lab is withdrawing fine-tuning, and tunable bases churn within weeks.

claims.raise_if: A tuned open model shown head to head against a current frontier model on the customer's own task, with cost, and still ahead three months later.
claims.lower_if: More tuned models overtaken by the next general release within a quarter, or more providers withdrawing tuning products.

claims.statement: Looping pays where weight memory binds. Running part of a model more than once per token buys quality per byte of weights at extra compute per token, so it suits a laptop or many models on one GPU; where compute or latency binds, a larger plain model beats a loop added after training.
claims.plain: A looped model is a smaller model that works harder on each word. That helps when memory is short and hurts when time is.
claims.why: For a provider serving many models, this decides whether looped models fit more models per GPU or are a slower road to quality that a bigger model gives more cheaply. Trained loops keep a cache for every pass over the prompt, which can cancel the saving on weights.

history.why: Opened when the reader asked whether looped models were covered. A check that priced the compute found loops added after training paying only at 0.8B, and a plain 14B beating a looped 8B on maths at modest extra time. Learned loops do match larger models per byte, and one lab built a looped model to fit a laptop. Against: that lab also claims a per-compute win for loops learned in training, and nobody has served a looped and a dense model of equal quality side by side.

claims.raise_if: A looped and a dense model of equal quality served in one engine, with the looped one ahead where weights limit what fits and behind where cache or compute does.
claims.lower_if: A loop added after training beating a larger model at equal decoding time, or a looped model ahead of a dense one of equal compute on throughput per GPU at equal quality.
